abstract: We present an algebraic algorithm that computes the composition of two power series in softly linear time complexity. The previous best algorithms are $\mathop{\mathrm{O}}(n^{1+o(1)})$ non-algebraic algorithm by Kedlaya and Umans (FOCS 2008) and an $\mathop{\mathrm{O}}(n^{1.43})$ algebraic algorithm by Neiger, Salvy, Schost and Villard (JACM 2023). Our algorithm builds upon the recent Graeffe iteration approach to manipulate rational power series introduced by Bostan and Mori (SOSA 2021).

Abstract—We present an algebraic algorithm that computes
the composition of two power series in softly linear time complexity. The previous best algorithms are O(n1+o(1) ) non-algebraic
algorithm by Kedlaya and Umans (FOCS 2008) and an O(n1.43 )
algebraic algorithm by Neiger, Salvy, Schost and Villard (JACM
2023).
Our algorithm builds upon the recent Graeffe iteration approach to manipulate rational power series introduced by Bostan
and Mori (SOSA 2021).
Index Terms—algebraic algorithms, computations on polynomials

I. I NTRODUCTION
Let A be a commutative ring and let f (x), g(x) be polynomials in A[x] of degrees less than m and n, respectively.
The problem of power series composition is to compute the
coefficients of f (g(x)) mod xn . The terminology stems from
the idea that g(x) can be seen as a truncated formal power
series. This is a fundamental problem in computer algebra [21,
Section 4.7], and has applications in various areas such as
combinatorics [24] and cryptography [4].
A textbook algorithm for power series composition is due
to Brent and Kung [9], which computes the composition in
O(M(n)(n log n)1/2 ) time complexity. Here M(n) denotes the
complexity of computing the product of two polynomials of
degree less than n.
The current best known algorithm for power series composition is due to Kedlaya and Umans [19], [20], which
computes the composition in (n log q)1+o(1) bit operations,
where A is the finite field Fq . Van der Hoeven and Lecerf
[32] gave a detailed analysis of the subpolynomial term,
and showed
that the algorithm has a time complexity of

In this paper, we present a simple algorithm that reduces the
complexity of power series composition to near-linear time.
Furthermore, our algorithm works over arbitrary commutative
rings.
Theorem 1: Given polynomials f (x), g(x) ∈ A[x] with
degree less than m and n, respectively, the power series composition f (g(x)) mod xn can be computed in O(M(n) log m+
M(m)) arithmetic operations.
We remark that our algorithm also has consequences for
other computation models measured by bit complexity, such
as boolean circuits and multitape Turing machines.

A. Related Work
a) Special Cases.: Many previous works have focused on
special cases where f and/or g has a specific form. Kung [22]
applied Newton iteration to compute the reciprocal of a power
series, i.e., f = (1 + x)−1 , in O(M(n)) operations, Brent
[8] further extended the algorithm for f being elementary
functions. Extensive work has been done to further optimize
the constant factor of the algorithms computing reciprocals
[1], [16], [26]–[28], square roots [1], [16], [28], exponentials
[1], [7], [15], [28], [29], [31], and other elementary functions.
Gerhard [14] gave an O(M(n) log n) algorithm for the case
when g(x) = ex − 1 and g(x) = log(1 + x), which can be
interpreted as the conversion between the falling factorial basis
and the monomial basis of polynomials. Brent and Kung [9]
showed that when g(x) is a constant degree polynomial, the
composition can be computed in O(M(n) log n) time. This
result is generalized by van der Hoeven [30] to the case where
g(x) is an algebraic power series. Bostan, Salvy and Schost [6]
isolated a large class of g such that the composition problem
can be computed in O(M(n) log n) or O(M(n)) operations,
by composing several basic subroutines and the usage of the
transposition principle [3].
Bernstein [2] studied the composition of a power series in
the case where A has a small characteristic. When A has
positive characteristic q, his algorithm computes the composition of a power series in O((q/ log q) M(n) log n) operations.
Ritzmann [25] studied the numerical algorithm of power series
composition, where A is the field of complex numbers.
b) Modular Composition.: Besides Brent and Kung’s
O(M(n)(n log n)1/2 )-time algorithm, all known approaches
toward the general power series composition, actually solve a
generalized problem called the modular composition problem.
This problem is, given three polynomials f (x), g(x), h(x) ∈
A[x] where h is monic, to compute f (g) mod h where the
mod operation takes the remainder of the Euclidean division.
When restricted to h(x) = xn , the modular composition
problem becomes the power series composition problem.
In Brent and Kung’s paper [9] on power series composition,
they also presented an algorithm that computes modular composition in O(n(ω+1)/2 + M(n)(n log n)1/2 ) operations, where
ω is a feasible exponent of matrix multiplication. Huang and
Pan [18] improved the bound to O(nω2 /2 + M(n)(n log n)1/2 )
by using the fast rectangular matrix multiplication, where
ω2 ≤ ω + 1 is a feasible exponent of rectangular matrix
multiplication of size n × n2 × n. Even assuming one can

B. Computation Model
Informally, we measure the complexity of an algorithm
by counting the number of arithmetic operations in the ring
A. The underlying computation model is the straight-line
program. Readers are referred to the textbook of Bürgisser,
Clausen and Shokrollahi [10, Sec. 4.1] for a detailed explanation.

E. Transposition Principle
The transposition principle, a.k.a. Tellegen’s principle, is
an algorithmic theorem that allows one to produce a new
algorithm of the transposed problem of a given linear problem.
Theorem 5 ([10, Thm. 13.20]): Let M be an r × s matrix.
Suppose that there exists a linear straight-line program of
length L that computes the matrix-vector product b 7→ M b,
and M has z0 zero rows and z1 zero columns. Then the
transposed problem c 7→ M T c can be solved by a linear
straight-line program of length L − s + r − z1 + z0 .
Roughly speaking, the transposition principle allows one
to compute the transposed problem with the same time complexity as the original problem, provided that the algorithm
is A-linear, in the sense that only linear operations in the
coefficients of b are performed.
The transposed problem of power series composition is the
power projection problem, which is defined as follows.
Definition 1 (Power Projection): Given a positive integer m,
a polynomial g(x) of degree less than n, and a linear form
w : A[x]<n → A, the power projection problem is to compute
fi = w(g(x)i mod xn ) for all i = 0, . . . , m − 1. The linear
form
w is identified
by its values on the monomials xi , i.e.,

For a given polynomial g(x), consider the n × m matrix

problem is equivalent to computing M f , where f is the

problem is equivalent to computing M T b, where b is the
column vector of coefficients of the linear form w. It is
important to note that the power projection and composition
problems are linear only when the polynomial g is fixed, as
the output of these problems is nonlinear with respect to the
coefficients of g.

C. Polynomial Multiplication
Our algorithm calls polynomial multiplication as a crucial
subroutine. Over different rings, the time complexity of our
algorithm may vary due to the different polynomial multiplication algorithms.
For an effective ring A, we call a function MA (n) a
multiplication time for A[x] if polynomials in A[x] of degree
less than n can be multiplied in O(MA (n)) operations. When
the ring A is clear from the context, we simply write M(n).
Throughout this paper, we assume a regularity condition on
M(n), that for some constants α, β ∈ (0, 1), the function M
satisfies the condition M(⌈αn⌉) ≤ β M(n) for all sufficiently
large n. All the examples of M presented in this paper satisfy
this condition.
The fast Fourier transform (FFT) [12] gives the bound
when A is a field possessing roots of unity of sufficiently
high order; for example, the complex numbers C satisfies MC (n) = O(n log n). For any Fp -algebra A where
